item.title: Building Codeword: The Solver
item.description:
After building Anarchy Chess, I wanted a daily word game to pair with it and landed on Codeword. A codeword starts with an open 13x13 crossword grid (around 120 white squares) with all of the clues removed. Instead, every white square carries a number from #1 to #26. Those numbers form a 1-to-1 substitution cipher for the alphabet: each number stands for one distinct letter from A to Z, all 26 letters appear somewhere on the grid, and typing L onto #2 fills every #2 square across the board.

Only two to four starter letters are revealed at the start, so cracking the rest is all about spotting word patterns and crossing letters. Under the hood, the Go CSP solver builds each day’s grids, checks that a human can deduce all 26 letters step by step without guessing, proves no second solution exists, and powers hints.

item.title: Building Anarchy Chess: The Solver
item.description:
Way back in my first post on the solver, I used N-queens as a warm-up problem: place N queens on an NxN chessboard so none of them attack each other. Recently I turned a generalized version of that puzzle into a daily game called Anarchy Chess.

Instead of eight queens, each puzzle hands you a mixed tray of queens, rooks, bishops, and knights. In Anarchy mode, the board also comes with five immovable blocks: sliding pieces (queens, rooks, and bishops) stop at blocks, while knights jump right over them. Unlike the sudoku or crossword apps where you watch the solver show off, here you do the solving yourself while the Go CSP engine works backstage: verifying boards, cooking up balanced daily puzzles, and rescuing stuck players with hints.

item.title: Faster Search: Flattening State and Backjumping
item.description: In the first two posts of this series, I packed live domains into bitsets and moved constraint propagation to bulk bitmasks. Once those stopped dominating the CPU profile, the spotlight moved to everything wrapping the propagation loop: variable map lookups, mutexes, undoing prunings, and backjumping state.

item.title: Faster Search: Bitmask Constraint Propagation
item.description:
In the previous post, I replaced map-backed live domains with []uint64 bitsets. That makes checking and flipping individual domain values cheap, which is great, except the original propagation loop was still polling Supported() on every single remaining value one at a time.

When a word has 15,000 candidates, calling Supported() 15,000 times just to cross off a single candidate is a lot of wasted work. In this post I’ll flip that around: letting constraints push prunings directly in bulk, and using precomputed bitmasks (bit patterns stored in uint64 slices) to filter thousands of candidates at once.

item.title: Faster Search: Live Domains as Bitsets
item.description:
For a long time my CSP solver was “fast enough”, mostly because I threw 9x9 Sudokus and relatively tame crosswords at it. Recently I started pushing the crossword builder harder: larger word lists, full arc consistency, and searching for higher-scoring word fills instead of stopping at the first valid grid. My poor free-tier GCE VM was not thrilled.

Profiling made the bottleneck obvious. The solver was spending more time hashing Go maps, allocating temporary state, and checking words one by one than actually exploring the search tree. Over a series of posts, I’ll walk through the recent changes that fixed that:

  1. Packing live domains into bitsets (this post).
  2. Bitmask constraint propagation instead of checking values one by one.
  3. Flattening search state from Go maps into dense slices, and speeding up backjumping along the way.

item.title: Building the Crossword Builder
item.description: My crossword builder is essentially composed of two major parts: the frontend and the backend. The frontend is in JavaScript, while the backend is written in Go. In this post I’ll talk about how each side works, and how the two communicate with each other.

item.title: All Different Variants
item.description:
In the earlier posts I’ve described some of the basic ideas behind CSPs:

  • how the problems are represented using variables and constraints,
  • how the solver searches for a solution by building up the search tree,
  • how heuristics guide the search, and
  • how constraint propagation helps eliminate parts of the search space that will not contain solutions.

In this post I will look at how modeling the problem itself can have a significant influence on how quickly the solver is able to find a solution. In particular, I’ll talk about different ways of implementing the all-different constraint, and look at the various implementations’ performance characteristics.

item.title: Visualizing Search
item.description:
Part of the appeal of building a solver for the fourth time (?!) for me is that it’s fun to watch how it solves the problem. While it’s possible and quick to hack something up on command line, the results aren’t that pretty and can’t be easily shared. In this post I’ll talk about building a frontend that talks to the backend via websockets and produces an animated visualization of how the search is solving the problem.

The scope of this post, and my initial frontend, is generalized NxN sudokus, and this first iteration of the frontend focused on largely non-interactive visualization. You can try it out for yourself online. I’ll talk about building up more interactive solvers for regular sudoku and crosswords separately.

item.title: Heuristics
item.description:
Constructive search needs to explore an exponentially large search space. In order to have any hope to find a solution, or prove that none exist, it is crucial that this exploration is done in a smart way. Problems that constructive search is applied to are NP-complete, so we don’t have an exact way of making smart decisions about this exploration. Instead, we rely on heuristics to make generally good decisions, that will hopefully help us either find a solution, or prove that one does not exist quickly.

There are two categories of these heuristics - variable ordering heuristics, and value ordering heuristics. Let’s take a closer look at how they work.

item.title: Constraint Propagation
item.description:
Constraint propagation is one of the key mechanisms that allows constructive search to efficiently explore huge search spaces. It does so by applying constraints whenever search state changes to remove parts of search space that cannot contain solutions.

In this post I’ll cover two constraint propagation techniques: forward checking and arc consistency. As these techniques apply to variables’ live domains, I’ll start by defining what that is first, and then dive into constraint propagation itself.
